questions.prompt: Anthropic's guide lists four qualities of good success criteria. Which list matches it?

options.text: Short, positive, approved by the vendor, and the same for every team.
options.explanation: The guide doesn't list these. Its four qualities are about what you measure and why.
Right. For example, "accurate sentiment classification" is more specific than "good performance".

options.text: Fast, cheap, private and always 100% accurate.
options.explanation: Speed, price and privacy can be criteria, but they are not the four qualities. The guide also says targets must be achievable.

questions.prompt: In Anthropic's sentiment example, what rule does it set for errors?

options.text: No errors at all are allowed in month one.
options.explanation: The example sets no such rule. It accepts some errors and limits how bad they are, with plenty of room for either choice.

options.text: 90% of errors may only cause inconvenience.
options.explanation: Right. The guide adds that you would also define what "inconvenience" and "egregious" mean.

options.text: Half of all errors must be fixed within a day.
options.explanation: The example says nothing about fixing times for errors, only about how bad they are.

questions.prompt: Anthropic's post on evals says who is best placed to define success. Who?

options.text: The people closest to product requirements and users, such as product managers.
options.explanation: Right. The post also names customer success managers and salespeople.

options.text: Only the engineers who build the system, because they know how it works.
options.explanation: The post says two engineers can read the same spec differently. It points to the people closest to users.

options.text: The model vendor, because it knows its own model best.
options.explanation: The vendor doesn't know your users or your costs. The post points to people close to your product.
